newsitem.title: USA: Specter fears Conrail deal means job loss.
newsitem.headline: Specter fears Conrail deal means job loss.

text.p: Sen. Arlen Specter said Friday he fears the proposed acquisition of Conrail and its division would cost thousands of jobs in Pennsylvania and mean the shutdown of company headquarters in Philadelpia.

At a news conference, the Pennsylvania Republican urged the Surface Transportation Board, the federal agency that regulates railroads, to "give ample weight" to those factors as it considers whether to approve the acquisition.
Specter, noting he was also concerned that rail lines serving coal companies in the western part of the state might shut down, said he may conduct hearings on the deal.

Philadelphia-based Conrail is negotiating a transaction to be acquired by CSX Corp. for $10.3 billion, or $115 per share. Conrail, which has an existing pact with CSX, is seeking to revise the deal in order to match a rival bid from Norfolk Southern Corp.. That would set the stavision of Conrail's assets between CSX and Norfolk.

"I write to express my deep concern about reports of a proposed division of Conrail between CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern," Specter said in a letter to Surface Transportation Board Chairman Linda Morgan.
Specter also released text of a letter to John Snow, chief executive officer of CSX.

"I am very troubled that CSX Corporation has breached a commitment it made to me that any arrangement would protect both the corporate headquarters in Pennsylvania and the dedicated employees throughout the commonwealth," Specter wrote.
Specter promised reporters he would identify who made that commitment to him and when it was made.

Specter has no direct means of stopping the deal, although he said a lawsuit may be possible under Pennsylvania law. He also noted pointedly that he sits on an appropriations subcommittee that funds the Surface Transportation Board.

"In this era of megamergers, I believe that is in the public interest that relatively small companies like Conrail ought to be retained," he wrote to Morgan. But he said later that he does not necessarily oppose a merger, so long as his concerns are addressed.
